```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)    # `read_html()` for the NSDUH web table
library(readxl)   # `read_excel()` for the LOTR spreadsheet
```

## Functions!

Start small with Z scores.

```{r}
# `rnorm()` draws random values from a normal distribution: n values, with this mean and sd.
# The values change every run; add `set.seed()` with any number above this line to get the same values every time.

x_vec = rnorm(n = 40, mean = 12, sd = 63)

# Z score = (value - mean) / sd: how many SDs each value is from the mean

(x_vec - mean(x_vec)) / sd(x_vec)
```

Let's turn this into a function.

```{r}
# `function(x)` creates a function with one ARGUMENT, x (the input).
# The code inside { } runs each time the function is called.

z_scores = function(x) {
  
 # Input checks: `stop()` halts the function with a custom error message
  
 if (!is.numeric(x)) {                     # ! means "not": runs if x is NOT numeric
   stop("Input x must be numeric")
 } else if(length(x) < 5) {                # checked only if the first condition was FALSE
   stop("x should have 5 or more numbers")
 }
  
 z = (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)                 # the same Z score calculation as above
  
  return(z)                                # `return()` sends the result back as the output
 
}
```

Does this actually work?

```{r}
z_scores(x_vec)
z_scores(rpois(4000, lambda = 12))   # `rpois()` draws random counts from a Poisson distribution with mean lambda
```

Don't run these on knitting

```{r eval = FALSE}
# `eval = FALSE` shows this code without running it, since each line triggers an error by design

z_scores(iris)                         # a dataframe, not a numeric vector -> "must be numeric"
z_scores("my name is emanuel")         # text -> "must be numeric"
z_scores(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE))  # logical values don't count as numeric -> "must be numeric"
z_scores(3)                            # numeric, but only 1 value -> "5 or more numbers"
```

## Mean and SD

```{r}
mean(x_vec)
sd(x_vec)
```

Write a function that returns the mean and sd of an input vector.

```{r}
# `source()` runs another R script, so the functions defined in it become available here.
# Keeping functions in separate files keeps this document shorter and lets other files reuse them.

source("source/mean_and_sd.R")
```

Check that this works

```{r}
mean_and_sd(x_vec)
```

## Motivate and Write Another One

```{r}
source("source/sim_mean_sd.R")
```

```{r}
# R matches arguments to a function either by NAME or by POSITION

sim_mean_sd(n_obs = 4000, mu = 12, sigma = 3)   # named: order doesn't matter

sim_mean_sd(4000, 12, 3)                        # positional matching: values match arguments in the order they're defined

mean(x_vec)

sim_mean_sd(50)   # only n_obs given; mu and sigma use their DEFAULT values set in the function definition
```

## Fix Things That Bother Me

Jeff said in class this bothered him:

```{r}
source("source/asdf.R") # what you name the R script does not matter, so long as the path in `source()` matches the file name

# The same import-and-tidy steps for three movies, written once as a function and called three times.
# Only the inputs change: which cells to read and which movie label to add.

fellowship_df =
  lotr_import(cell_range = "B3:D6", movie_title = "fellowship")

two_towers_df =
  lotr_import(cell_range = "F3:H6", movie_title = "two_towers")

return_df =
  lotr_import(cell_range = "J3:L6", movie_title = "return_of_king")
```

```{r}
source("source/nsduh_process.R")

url = "https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/NSDUHsaeShortTermCHG2015/NSDUHsaeShortTermCHG2015.htm"
drug_use_html = read_html(url)   # download the page once, then reuse it for every table

# `nsduh_process()` pulls one table from the page by its position `(table_num)` and cleans it,
# replacing the copy-and-paste code from the web scraping lecture

marj_df =
  nsduh_process(html = drug_use_html, table_num = 1)
  
cocaine_df =
  nsduh_process(html = drug_use_html, table_num = 4)
  
heroin_df =
  nsduh_process(html = drug_use_html, table_num = 5)
```
